card.hook: Picture a red-tiled campus, a stone arch, and the Flatirons standing behind it like they were put there on purpose. All you need is one person to walk into the opening.
card.stand_here: Stand on the lawn of Farrand Field and face the arch at the top of the steps, with the Flatirons rising behind the campus. The campus lies to the north of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x so the arch, the person and the mountains all fit. Try 2x if you want the Flatirons to look bigger behind the arch, and save 0.5x for shots of the whole lawn (keep the horizon level).
card.make_it_pop: Tap the person in the arch, then slide the brightness down a little so the sky and mountains keep their colour.
card.best_time: Go in spring or autumn, when the trees are in bloom or changing colour. They make the warm sandstone look even better.
card.selfie_here: For a selfie, stand beside the Ralphie buffalo statue directly outside Folsom Field with the stadium behind you, or on the wide Norlin Library steps with its columns behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x to fit more in, and hold the phone a bit low so the landmark sits over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the Norlin Quad grass facing the Norlin Steps, far enough back to fit the whole library, while you pose on the steps (it's worth checking this spot on the map first).
card.rules_and_safety: The campus is a working university, and the area around Old Main has reportedly been under construction, so check the official site to see whether access is open. The Norlin Steps can get very busy during graduation season.
card.challenge: Be patient and wait for a stranger to stroll into the arch, then snap it before they step out. Bonus points if the Flatirons stay perfectly level.
card.good_to_know: The university was founded in 1876, five months before Colorado became a state. Old Main's cornerstone was laid in 1875 and its doors opened in 1877. Most buildings share one look, Tuscan Vernacular Revival, planned by architect Charles Klauder, with sandstone from quarries across the Front Range.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the lawn of Farrand Field and face the arch at the top of the steps, with the Flatirons rising behind the campus. The campus lies to the north of you.

card.hook: Picture a smooth paved path, a creek chuckling beside it, and the tilted Flatirons rising over the trees. The only tricky part is getting a moment when no cyclist is zooming through.
card.stand_here: Head for Scott Carpenter Park and stand by the creek path, facing the Flatirons so they rise behind it. If it doesn't line up, stroll a short way along the path and try again.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the path and the Flatirons in one shot. Tap 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to bring the rock slabs closer, or 0.5x if you want lots of sky and trees.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the path along the lower third so it leads to the Flatirons, then tap the Flatirons and slide a little darker so the sky and rock keep their detail.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the rock. Spring and early summer bring high, fast water, so keep well back from the edge.
card.selfie_here: Try the path beside the Boulder Public Library, a few blocks south of Pearl Street, and hold your front camera so the long path stretches out behind you. For a shadier look, Central Park (1236 Canyon Blvd) has stone bridges nearby and a flat paved path, so try 0.5x to squeeze it all in.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the paved path beside the Boulder Public Library and frame you against the path's length and the creek.
card.rules_and_safety: Several road crossings on the path need caution, so take care when stopping for photos near them. Keep children and bags back from the creek banks, and check conditions when you arrive.
card.challenge: Can you get the whole path looking calm and empty? Wait for the gap between cyclists and walkers, or take a Live Photo and pick your favourite frame afterwards.
card.good_to_know: Boulder Creek Path is the paved trail that follows Boulder Creek through the city. The Flatirons are the tilted slabs of rock above the town. For a different shot, Eben G. Fine Park has creekside boulders and reflections, and Central Park has cottonwoods, stone bridges and dappled light close to downtown.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head for Scott Carpenter Park and stand by the creek path, facing the Flatirons so they rise behind it. If it doesn't line up, stroll a short way along the path and try again.

card.hook: Picture a settler staring up at these huge tilted slabs and thinking, "Looks like an old clothes iron." That's how the Flatirons got their name, and once you see the sloping shapes you can't unsee it.
card.stand_here: Stand in the open meadow in front of the Ranger Cottage at Chautauqua Park, then turn to face due west, where the Flatirons rise. From here the whole line of slabs sits behind a green foreground of grass and, in season, wildflowers.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the full line of slabs. Switch to 0.5x if you want more meadow in the foreground, or try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out a single slab.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the strip of grass on the lower third line, and crouch a little so grasses or flowers sit in front while the rock fills the rest of the frame.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning. The rock faces east, so it catches the first direct light then, and the slabs fall into shadow later in the day.
card.selfie_here: Take your selfie on the meadow directly in front of the Ranger Cottage. The slabs rise almost straight above you, so they fill the background behind your shoulder. Use the front camera and hold it a bit low so the rock fits in. For a calmer, cleaner backdrop, the open grass fields at the Flatirons Vista trailhead, at the south end of Boulder, have no buildings in the frame.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand well back from the rock on the open meadow and shift sideways until the individual slabs no longer overlap behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Parking rules and trail access can change, and some photo sessions may need a permit, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Get all five slabs, First to Fifth, in one frame with no overlaps, then count them out loud like you're taking a register.
card.good_to_know: The rock is roughly 290 to 296 million years old. It was pushed up and tipped on its side long ago, then uncovered by erosion. Today the five numbered slabs, First to Fifth, run north to south and are Boulder's signature backdrop.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in the open meadow in front of the Ranger Cottage at Chautauqua Park, then turn to face due west, where the Flatirons rise. From here the whole line of slabs sits behind a green foreground of grass and, in season, wildflowers.

card.hook: There's nearly always something going on along Pearl Street Mall, whether it's a fountain, a sculpture or a magician pulling a coin from somebody's ear. It's a street where the photo is half the fun and the people-watching is the other half.
card.stand_here: Stand near Broadway, about 180 m west of the numbered pin, at the phone icon on the map. Face east so the street runs away from you with buildings on both sides.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x for the long street view and the public art, then switch to 1x for people and shopfronts. Use zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for performers and details from a polite distance.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the street up with the centre or a third of the frame, then add a sculpture, a flowerbed or a few passers-by in the foreground to show scale.
card.best_time: Come in spring for the tulips or in summer for the street performers. Late afternoon into evening gives warm light, a livelier crowd and shop and restaurant lights switching on. After dark, use night mode and rest your phone against a wall or railing.
card.selfie_here: Try the bronze buffalo sculpture on the sidewalk outside the Boulder Bookstore. Use the front camera, pop it to 0.5x if your phone has it, and check what's behind your shoulder before you tap, because we haven't confirmed how much of the mall shows there. Another option is the decorative bridge over the mall where the dragonfly sculpture sits.
card.ask_someone: Stand on the Boulder County Courthouse lawn on the north side of the 1300 block and ask a passer-by to shoot you with the courthouse behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Please ask before photographing or filming performers up close, and keep clear of the middle of the walkway so people can pass. Check the official site before you go for any events or closures.
card.challenge: Find the stylised map of Boulder County in the street art and get a shot with it in the foreground and the street stretching out behind.
card.good_to_know: Pearl Street Mall is four car-free blocks, from 11th Street to 15th Street. It was built between June 1976 and August 1977 and officially dedicated on 6 August 1977. One of its designers cited a 1945 French film about busy Parisian streets and buskers as inspiration, which explains the lively, people-first feel.

card.hook: Hotel Boulderado opened on New Year's Day 1909, the morning after a gala ball, and its long, solid front still looks ready for a party. It's an easy, honest street photo of old Boulder.
card.stand_here: Head for the phone icon near 13th Street, about 20 m west of the numbered pin, and face east toward the hotel. You'll be fairly close, so take a step or two back if the whole frontage doesn't fit.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the full length of the building. Then try 1x for a more natural look, and 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for upper windows and signs.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line up the edge of the building with a vertical line, so the walls stand straight instead of leaning.
card.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light is kind to this building. At dusk the lit windows and entrance glow, so switch on night mode and brace your phone against a wall or post.
card.selfie_here: Stand on the pavement in front of the main entrance at 13th and Spruce, facing the front doors, with the brick façade behind you. Use the front camera, and try 0.5x if your phone offers it so more of the hotel fits over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Stand on the pavement in front of the main entrance and ask a passer-by to step back until the whole façade, including the corner, fits in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: The outside is fine to photograph from the street. The hotel is a working business, so check its official site before taking photos inside, and be polite to guests and staff.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot where the building's edge sits dead on a gridline, then sneak in close for a shot of a window, a sign or some brickwork.
card.good_to_know: The hotel was designed by local architects Redding & Sons, who mixed Italian Renaissance and Spanish Colonial Revival styles. Inside, the stained-glass lobby ceiling was designed to echo the one in San Francisco's Palace Hotel, and the original 1908 Otis elevator is still in use. It joined Historic Hotels of America in 1996.

card.hook: There's a bronze buffalo standing guard outside Gate 1, and he's a regular stop on campus tours. Make him the star of your Folsom Field photo and let the stadium be the backdrop.
card.stand_here: Stand at the Monarch of the Plains statue, outside Gate 1 on the Balch Fieldhouse courtyard side. Face the statue so the stadium entrance and campus buildings sit behind it. The main part of Folsom Field lies to the north-east.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the buffalo with the entrance behind him. Switch to 0.5x for more of the brick frontage, or 2x and up to pick out details on the bronze figure.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the buffalo on one third line, and crouch a little so he stands out against the buildings.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the bronze and fewer people in the courtyard. Match days and event days are busy, so give yourself extra time and be patient.
card.selfie_here: Take it at the Ralphie buffalo statue outside Folsom Field, which is the most popular photo spot here. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and tuck the stadium in over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Stand beside the buffalo statue and ask a passer-by to shoot from the street or walkway in front of it, so the whole stadium fits behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The statue is outside the stadium, but the stadium itself is generally open only for events, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Get the buffalo on a third line with the entrance behind him and not a single stranger walking through the shot.
card.good_to_know: The stadium opened in 1924 as Colorado Stadium and was renamed Folsom Field in 1944, after former head coach Fred Folsom. It's horseshoe-shaped and opens to the north. At 5,360 feet (1,635 m), it sits more than a mile above sea level.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the Monarch of the Plains statue, outside Gate 1 on the Balch Fieldhouse courtyard side. Face the statue so the stadium entrance and campus buildings sit behind it. The main part of Folsom Field lies to the north-east.

card.hook: You walk into the meadow at Colorado Chautauqua and the Flatirons are right there, huge tilted slabs of sandstone leaning over the grass. Most people stop, look up and say "wow" before they've even got their phone out.
card.stand_here: Stand in the meadow in front of Ranger Cottage and face the Flatirons, which loom almost directly overhead from here. Don't stress about the exact spot, because the whole meadow works.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the meadow and the rocks in one frame, then try 1x for a calmer view. Tap 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the rock faces.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the rocks, then drag the slider towards darker so the bright sky doesn't wash out the sandstone.
card.best_time: Go at sunrise, when the Flatirons face the first light and glow. Late afternoon often leaves them in shadow.
card.selfie_here: Take your selfie in the open meadow in front of Ranger Cottage, with the Flatirons rising above you. Use the front camera, switch to the wider front view if your phone has one, and hold it a bit low so the rocks fill the space over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand in the meadow below the rocks and frame you against the 1898 Chautauqua Auditorium, with you standing in front of it.
card.rules_and_safety: Commercial photography in the Flatirons area needs a City of Boulder Open Space and Mountain Parks photo permit, but that's for professional shoots, not casual visitor photos like yours.
card.challenge: Get down low so the meadow grass fills the bottom of your frame and the Flatirons tower above it. Bonus points if you keep the horizon dead level.
card.good_to_know: Colorado Chautauqua began in 1898 as a summer school and lecture series, and it still runs talks, concerts and silent films all year. The whole 40-acre site, with its historic cottages, dining hall and auditorium, became a National Historic Landmark in 2006. The grounds and the adjoining park are open to the public with no entry fee.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in the meadow in front of Ranger Cottage and face the Flatirons, which loom almost directly overhead from here. Don't stress about the exact spot, because the whole meadow works.

card.hook: Here's a secret about Flagstaff Mountain: you don't photograph it, you stand on it and photograph everything else. The whole of Boulder is laid out below you like a model town.
card.stand_here: Head to Panorama Point, the first pullout on the right going up Flagstaff Road from Baseline Road. Face out over Boulder and the eastern plains, so the summit is behind you to the west.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the main view over Boulder, then go to 0.5x to catch the whole sweep of the plains. Try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out streets and rooftops below.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, keep the horizon level with the town in the lower half, then tap the town and make the screen a touch darker at sunset so the sky keeps its colour.
card.best_time: Sunrise and sunset are the stars here, when the town and plains pick up softer colour. Check the road gate times first, because the summit road closes in the evening and you don't want to be out until full dark.
card.selfie_here: For a selfie with rock behind you, walk about 0.1 miles from the Lost Gulch Overlook parking area to the rock outcrop you can sit on. Use the front camera and hold it a little high so the sandstone and pines fill the background. At Panorama Point, the stone overlook works too, with the slope and the Flatirons behind you, though the mountain shows less clearly there.
card.ask_someone: Down at Chautauqua Park, at the base of the mountain off Baseline Road, ask a passer-by to take your photo while you stand on the open grassy field.
card.rules_and_safety: The road up has steep inclines and hairpin turns, and cyclists use it, so take it slowly. Flagstaff Summit Road is seasonal and closes in the evening, and vehicles not registered in Boulder County may need a parking permit or fee, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Zoom in to 2x or more and find one rooftop or street in Boulder below, then try to get it perfectly sharp in your photo.
card.good_to_know: Flagstaff Mountain rises straight up from the western edge of Boulder. It's part of Boulder Mountain Park in the Flatirons region, on the eastern flank of the Front Range. The summit stands at 6,983 feet (2,128 m).
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head to Panorama Point, the first pullout on the right going up Flagstaff Road from Baseline Road. Face out over Boulder and the eastern plains, so the summit is behind you to the west.

card.hook: Everyone shoots the famous sandstone towers from the front. Follow the NCAR trail past the big green water tank and you get a quieter, wilder view with Bear Peak rising over the grass.
card.stand_here: Stand on the Mesa Trail vista, about 1 km to the north-west of the building, on the trail west of the laboratory. Face south to Bear Canyon and Bear Peak, with grassland and pines in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x for the big sweep of foothills, grass and pines. Switch to 1x for a balanced shot of Bear Peak. Try 2x-5x (depends on your phone) to pull the laboratory and the Flatirons closer together.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the mountains, then slide the brightness a little darker so the sky keeps its colour.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon gives softer, warmer light on the hills and the building. Spring is your moment if you want wildflowers at your feet.
card.selfie_here: Walk the short mesa trails directly behind the Mesa Laboratory. Within a couple of minutes you get open grass and sky, so use the front camera at 0.5x and keep the towers over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand in the free parking lot at the top of the grounds and shoot toward the building, while you pose along the paved path that runs from the lot to the building.
card.rules_and_safety: Wear proper shoes and bring water. Summer afternoons on the mesa can be hot and exposed, and thunderstorms can develop quickly. Check trail conditions and public access before you go, because summer storms and snow can affect access and the lab's public access can change.
card.challenge: Turn on the gridlines, tuck some grass or pine branches into the bottom of the frame, and put Bear Peak off-centre.
card.good_to_know: The National Center for Atmospheric Research was founded in 1960 and is still headquartered at its Mesa Laboratory. It is sponsored by the National Science Foundation and managed by the University Corporation for Atmospheric Research. The angular sandstone towers were designed by I.M. Pei.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the Mesa Trail vista, about 1 km to the north-west of the building, on the trail west of the laboratory. Face south to Bear Canyon and Bear Peak, with grassland and pines in front of you.

selfie_spots.why: The short mesa trails behind the building trade that hard architecture for scrubby grass and open sky within a couple of minutes. That keeps the building as the backdrop while the foreground stays uncrowded.

card.hook: Walk around central Boulder and then, bang, there's a building that looks nothing like anything near it. That's the Dushanbe Teahouse, and it's a photo-stopper before you've even found the door.
card.stand_here: Go to the park opposite the teahouse (Central Park, though your map may call it Boulder Creek Park) and walk about 68 m north-east towards the front of the building. Stop when the whole colourful front fills your view, and face it head-on.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to fit the whole front in with the park around it. Try 0.5x only if you want more park and sky, and keep the building away from the edges so it doesn't stretch. Use 2x for the tile panels if your phone has it.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line the building's edges up with them so the walls stand straight, with a bit of lawn or snow along the bottom of the frame.
card.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light suits the colours best. Come in the warmer months if you want the rose beds and entry garden at their fullest.
card.selfie_here: Walk over to the entrance and stand in front of one of the eight ceramic panels, so the painted walls are behind you. Use the front camera, hold it a little below eye level, and tap your face so you stay bright.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand in the park across from the teahouse so the full building fits in the frame, while you stand in front of it near the entrance.
card.rules_and_safety: The park and the Boulder Creek Path are public open space, but the teahouse is a working restaurant, so check the official site before you go if you want to see inside.
card.challenge: Find all eight ceramic panels and see if you can get a different one in the background of every selfie.
card.good_to_know: The teahouse was a gift to Boulder in 1987 from its sister city, Dushanbe in Tajikistan. Forty Tajik artisans spent about two years making it by hand, then packed it into roughly 200 crates. It took years to raise the money to put it up, and it finally opened to the public in 1998.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Go to the park opposite the teahouse (Central Park, though your map may call it Boulder Creek Park) and walk about 68 m north-east towards the front of the building. Stop when the whole colourful front fills your view, and face it head-on.

card.hook: Picture a glowing marquee against a darkening sky, with a pastel art deco front sitting on a quiet bit of 14th Street. That's the Boulder Theater at dusk, and it's an easy one to love.
card.stand_here: Stand on the street right in front of the Boulder Theater on 14th Street, about half a block off Pearl Street. The phone icon on the map is already in the right place. Face the building and aim at the marquee.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the facade and marquee together. If the pavement is narrow and the whole front won't fit, drop to zoom 0.5x. Use zoom 2x when you just want the marquee lettering.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the marquee, then slide it a little darker so the lights glow instead of turning white, and keep your gridlines on so the building's vertical lines stay straight.
card.best_time: Go at dusk or after dark, when the marquee lights are on and the facade is lit. Night mode will help, so hold your phone steady against your body or a wall for a second or two.
card.selfie_here: Stand on the sidewalk right at the marquee, at 2032 14th St, with the sign behind you. Travel Boulder says artists and fans often pose there with the marquee as their backdrop. Use the front camera, try zoom 0.5x if your phone offers it, and let the marquee show over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the Pearl Street Mall facing the theater's front so the whole building fits, while you pose on the sidewalk by the marquee.
card.rules_and_safety: You can photograph the front from the public street. If you step back across the street for the whole building, only do it when it's safe, and check the official site before going inside.
card.challenge: Take a few frames and catch the marquee with no pedestrian or passing car in the shot. Patience wins this one.
card.good_to_know: The building opened in 1906 as the Curran Opera House. In 1936 it became a cinema called the Boulder Theater, and its art deco look was inspired by the nearby Boulder courthouse. It closed in 1983, reopened in 1988 after a big renovation, and still hosts live acts today.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the street right in front of the Boulder Theater on 14th Street, about half a block off Pearl Street. The phone icon on the map is already in the right place. Face the building and aim at the marquee.

card.hook: That big Fox sign and the marquee? They're the originals, left over from when this place was a cinema, and they still steal the show on a busy Hill sidewalk.
card.stand_here: Stand on the pavement in front of 1135 13th St, directly facing the Fox Theatre's street-facing front. Face north-west, toward the building, and step back until the whole front fits.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for a natural, straight-on view. If the pavement is crowded and you can't step back far enough, try zoom 0.5x to fit it all in. Zoom 2x or 5x (higher zooms depend on your phone) gets you a close-up of the sign or marquee.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on the gridlines and line up the building's vertical edges with them so the front doesn't lean, with the sign and marquee in the top half and the entrance below.
card.best_time: Daytime gives you the clearest straight-on view of the front. If the sign is lit, evening can add some colour, so try night mode and rest your phone against a wall or post to keep it steady.
card.selfie_here: Flip to the front camera, try 0.5x if your phone has it, and hold it at arm's length so the sign and marquee sit over your shoulder. Tilt the phone up a little so the lettering makes it into the shot.
card.rules_and_safety: The Hill is busy, so expect passers-by, and sidewalk activity can block your view. It's a working music venue, so check the official site before you go if you want to head inside.
card.challenge: Wait for a gap in the crowd, then get the whole front in frame with the vertical edges lined up straight on the gridlines. Bonus points if the sign is perfectly centred.
card.good_to_know: The cinema opened in 1961, and when the old building was opened up in the early 1990s, work revealed its roots go back to 1926. The Fox opened as a live music venue on 6 March 1992 and seats just over 600 people. It marked its 30th anniversary in 2022.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the pavement in front of 1135 13th St, directly facing the Fox Theatre's street-facing front. Face north-west, toward the building, and step back until the whole front fits.

selfie_research.notes: No page I found names a specific vantage point for a selfie with the Fox Theatre behind the photographer, so I have left selfie_spots empty rather than guess. A Bandsintown review (https://www.bandsintown.com/v/10001134-fox-theatre) says the neon outside made for fun photo ops, but it names no street spot. The Wikipedia page (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fox_Theatre_(Boulder,_Colorado)) and the Advisor Travel page (https://en.advisor.travel/poi/Fox-Theatre-Boulder-Colorado-21759) place the theatre on 13th Street next to Tulagi's, between Five Guys and Tulagi's, across from the University of Colorado campus. Those are findable reference points, but neither page calls them a photo spot. The Advisor Travel page also places the box office across the street on the upper floor of Albums on The Hill, which could help a passer-by locate the frontage. No page I found gives a stand-in spot for taking a photo of a visitor with the whole front in frame, so ask_someone_spot is null. No page I found states selfie-stick or tripod rules or a safety point. The coordinates you gave match the Wikipedia coordinates to within a few tens of metres. Some listings give an older address, 2022 14th Street, for the venue's original 1960 site; the current address is 1135 13th Street. Only one search pass was possible, so a local photo-spot guide might still name a specific spot.

card.hook: This courthouse skips the frills. It's five storeys of straight lines and a tower, and that plain look is exactly what makes it fun to photograph.
card.stand_here: Stand at the corner of Pearl Street and 14th Street, at the west end of the mall. The courthouse is 67 m to the south-west, about 1 minute on foot, so turn to face south-west and let the street lead your eye to it.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to get the courthouse along the street. If the tower won't fit, tap 0.5x. For the tower and the lines of the facade, try 2x up to 5x, depending on your phone.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line one vertical line up with the tower or the building's edge, so the stonework stands up straight instead of leaning.
card.best_time: Go at sunset on a clear evening, when the low light warms the stone. The Flatirons may show behind the downtown blocks and catch some colour too, but check on the day.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera and tap 0.5x if your phone has it. Hold the phone a little low and tilt up so the courthouse tower rises over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: The mall and the street are open public space, but the courthouse is a working government building. Stick to public ground, and check the official site before you go if you want to go inside or photograph the grounds up close.
card.challenge: Take a shot where the tower sits dead straight against a vertical grid line. Then try the front lawn side, with the grass in front and the limestone behind it.
card.good_to_know: Architect Glen H. Huntington designed it in the WPA Moderne style, a restrained form of Art Deco, and it went up in 1933. It stands on the site of the 1882 courthouse, which burned down in 1932. In 1975 county clerk Clela Rorex issued marriage licences to six same-sex couples here, among the first in the US, and the building became a National Historic Landmark in 2024.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the corner of Pearl Street and 14th Street, at the west end of the mall. The courthouse is 67 m to the south-west, about 1 minute on foot, so turn to face south-west and let the street lead your eye to it.
